name: Grammar-constrained / structured-output decoding for guaranteed tool calls
what_it_is: A decoding technique that filters the model's token logits at every sampling step so only tokens that keep the output valid against a formal grammar can be emitted, guaranteeing the result conforms to a schema by construction. llama.cpp implements this as GBNF (GGML BNF) grammars, plus a json-schema-to-grammar converter; llama-server accepts either a raw 'grammar' body field, a 'json_schema' body field on completion endpoints, or OpenAI-style 'response_format': {'type':'json_schema', ...} on /chat/completions (the schema is used only to constrain output, not injected into the prompt). The same idea powers vLLM's guided decoding via XGrammar (pushdown-automaton, default) and Outlines (finite-state-machine) backends, exposed through guided_json / response_format json_schema. Because tool calls are just a JSON object matching the tool's parameter schema, grammar-constrained decoding can force structurally valid tool-call arguments.
real_precedent: llama.cpp GBNF + json-schema-to-grammar and llama-server json_schema/response_format support (https://deepwiki.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/8.1-grammar-and-structured-output ; https://deepwiki.com/qualcomm/llama.cpp/8-structured-output-and-function-calling); vLLM structured/guided decoding with XGrammar and Outlines (https://vllm-project.github.io/2025/01/14/struct-decode-intro.html); a concrete llama-server tool-calling bug report (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/22072).
evidence_of_impact: vLLM ships structured decoding as a first-class feature and defaults to XGrammar, reporting up to ~5x improvement in time-per-output-token under load vs the older Outlines path, and frames structured decoding as 'validation' that guarantees output matches expected formats without few-shot workarounds (https://vllm-project.github.io/2025/01/14/struct-decode-intro.html). llama.cpp exposes json_schema/response_format as standard llama-server body fields, showing production adoption of grammar-forced JSON (https://deepwiki.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/8.1-grammar-and-structured-output). [uncertain] A benchmark summary cited XGrammar one-shot JSON-schema success at ~60-78% vs Outlines ~93%, indicating backend-dependent reliability, but this single comparison was read from a search summary of https://blog.squeezebits.com/guided-decoding-performance-vllm-sglang and not independently reproduced.
applicability_to_agentdyno: AgentDyno already runs models behind llama-server and exposes a stable local OpenAI-compatible gateway (127.0.0.1:8403/v1), which is exactly where grammar constraints are applied. Today 'dyno doctor' P1-P3 tool-call probes passively grade whether a model emits well-formed tool calls; the same gateway could re-issue a failing probe with 'response_format':{'type':'json_schema'} (or a derived GBNF grammar) so the model is forced to emit a structurally valid tool call — turning some FAILs into structural PASSes and letting AgentDyno become an active 'fixer' (e.g., a 'dyno serve --force-tool-schema' or a doctor '--assist' mode that reports both raw grade and grammar-assisted grade). Crucially, doctor should report these as two distinct scores so users see 'model can do this unaided' vs 'model needs the harness to force structure' — that dual grade is itself a differentiator, and the assisted mode is a genuine remediation for Cline/Goose setups where malformed tool JSON otherwise breaks the agent loop.
build_effort: small-to-medium — the underlying capability already exists: llama-server accepts grammar/json_schema/response_format today, so the work is (1) generating a GBNF/json_schema from each probe's expected tool signature (json-schema-to-grammar handles most of this), (2) adding a gateway/serve toggle to inject it for tool-call requests, and (3) extending doctor to run each probe twice (unconstrained vs constrained) and emit a dual grade. Medium rather than small because of edge cases: per-model chat-template/tool-notation differences and schemas using regex/PCRE shorthands.
risk_or_caveat: Structural validity is not semantic correctness — a grammar guarantees well-formed JSON but the model can still fill it with wrong values or call the wrong tool, so a 'pass by construction' grade can be misleading and risks measuring the harness rather than the model. Over-constraining can degrade quality on reasoning-type tasks because the model can't 'think out loud' before committing to structure (effect is negligible for extraction/classification). Known limitations: llama.cpp's json-schema-to-grammar does not support PCRE shorthands (\d, \w, \s), uniqueItems, contains, if/then/else, or nested $ref, and can hit 'repetitions exceeds sane defaults' / slow-sampling gotchas on large tool grammars (https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/22314 ; https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/issues/22072); some models (e.g. Gemma-style fc notation) only get their structure forced, not their arguments, because the converter emits JSON rules, not the model's native tool notation. vLLM XGrammar likewise does not yet support regex or complex JSON patterns. So AgentDyno should treat grammar-forcing as a labeled remediation, not a way to silently inflate grades.
